sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll use the terminal that lives inside VS Code — instead of switching to a separate PowerShell window. You'll understand why this matters, how to open and close it, how to navigate with it, and how to run basic commands without leaving your editor.

This is one of the features that makes VS Code feel like a complete working environment rather than just a text editor.

## Why Have a Terminal Inside the Editor?

In lessons 4.3 and 4.4 you worked with a separate PowerShell window. That works fine, but it creates friction: you're constantly switching between two windows — the editor and the terminal.

VS Code's integrated terminal solves this. It's a full PowerShell (or bash on Mac) session running inside the same window as your code. You can see your code and your terminal at the same time, in the same place.

Practical benefits:
- **Starts in the right folder automatically.** The integrated terminal always opens in your project folder. No `cd` required to get to where you need to be.
- **No window switching.** Write code, run a command, see the result — without changing windows.
- **You can have multiple terminals open at once.** Each is a separate session.
- **It's the same terminal.** Everything you learned about PowerShell in Part 4 works exactly the same here.

From this lesson forward, use the integrated terminal whenever you need a command line while working in VS Code.

## Opening and Closing the Terminal

**To open the terminal:**
- Press **Ctrl+`** (the backtick key — top-left of the keyboard, directly under the Esc key, shares a key with the tilde ~)
- Or: click **Terminal** in the menu bar → **New Terminal**
- Or: use the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) → type `new terminal`

**To toggle it (show/hide):**
- Press **Ctrl+`** again — it hides the terminal panel. Press it again to show it.
- Or: press **Ctrl+J** to toggle the entire Panel section (which includes Terminal, Problems, Output)

**To close a specific terminal session:**
- Click the trash icon (🗑) in the terminal toolbar, or
- Type `exit` in the terminal and press Enter

The terminal appears at the bottom of the window as part of the Panel section.

**Can't find the backtick key?** On a standard keyboard it's in the top-left corner of the main key area, sharing a key with the tilde (~). It's directly to the left of the `1` key, and directly below the Esc key. If Ctrl+` doesn't work for you, use the menu: Terminal → New Terminal.

## The Terminal Starts in Your Project Folder

This is the key advantage of the integrated terminal. When VS Code opens a folder as a workspace, the terminal automatically starts in that same folder. You don't need to navigate.

Type `pwd` to confirm:
```
PS C:\Users\YourName\Documents\ai-course-projects>
```

The prompt shows you exactly where you are. If you open the terminal and see the wrong folder, it means VS Code was opened with a different folder (or no folder at all). Go back to File → Open Folder to open the right one.

**Basic navigation commands (from lesson 4.4):**
- `pwd` — print current directory (where am I?)
- `ls` — list files and folders here
- `cd foldername` — move into a subfolder
- `cd ..` — go up one level
- `cd ~` — go to your home folder (C:\Users\YourName)

## Multiple Terminals and Split Terminals

VS Code lets you have more than one terminal session running at the same time. This is useful when you want one terminal for running a server and another for general commands.

**Create a new terminal session:**
- Click the **+** button in the terminal toolbar (top-right of the terminal panel)
- Or: press Ctrl+Shift+` (Ctrl+Shift+backtick)

A new terminal tab appears. You can switch between them by clicking the tab names in the terminal panel's right sidebar.

**Split the terminal into two side-by-side panes:**
- Click the **split terminal** icon in the terminal toolbar (looks like a column split)
- Or: press **Ctrl+Shift+5**

Now you have two terminal sessions visible simultaneously, side by side. Click in either one to type in it.

**Close a terminal session:**
- Click the X next to its name in the terminal list, or type `exit`

sections.title: Terminal Inside VS Code
sections.content:
Complete these steps using only the integrated terminal inside VS Code. Do not open a separate PowerShell window.

**Step 1 — Open the terminal:**
1. Press **Ctrl+`** (backtick)
2. The terminal panel appears at the bottom of the window
3. Type `pwd` and press Enter
4. Confirm you see your `ai-course-projects` folder path

**Step 2 — Explore your project:**
1. Type `ls` and press Enter — you should see your folders: `exercises`, `notes`, `prompts`, and `README.md`
2. Type `cd exercises` and press Enter
3. Type `ls` — you should see `hello.html` and `part-05-notes.md`
4. Type `cd ..` to go back up to the project root

**Step 3 — Create a file from the terminal:**
1. Make sure you're at the project root (`pwd` should show `ai-course-projects`)
2. Type this command and press Enter:
   `echo "# My Notes" > notes/terminal-test.md`
3. In the Explorer panel, look inside the `notes` folder — `terminal-test.md` appeared!
4. Click it in the Explorer — it opens in the Editor Area with the text "# My Notes"

**Step 4 — Toggle and split the terminal:**
1. Press Ctrl+` to hide the terminal
2. Press Ctrl+` again to show it
3. Click the split icon in the terminal toolbar (or press Ctrl+Shift+5)
4. You now have two terminal panes side by side
5. Click in the right pane and type `ls` — it also shows your project files
6. Close the right pane by clicking its X

**Check:**
- [ ] Terminal opens and shows your project folder
- [ ] `ls` shows your folder structure
- [ ] `terminal-test.md` was created and appears in the Explorer
- [ ] You successfully toggled and split the terminal

sections.title: Workshop A — Integrated Terminal Drill
sections.content:
VS Code's integrated terminal is where you spend a lot of time. This drill builds fluency.

**Step 1 — Open the integrated terminal** (Ctrl+`).

**Step 2 — Practice these terminal operations:**
- Open a second terminal: click the + icon in the terminal panel
- Switch between terminals: click the terminal names in the dropdown
- Split the terminal: click the split icon — two terminals side-by-side
- Kill a terminal: click the trash icon

**Step 3 — Configure your terminal:**
- Click the dropdown arrow next to + → Select Default Profile → choose PowerShell or Git Bash
- Right-click the terminal area → Font Size → increase to a comfortable size

**Step 4 — Terminal useful shortcuts:**
- Ctrl+C: stop a running process
- Ctrl+L or `clear`: clear the terminal screen
- Up arrow: recall previous commands
- Tab: autocomplete file/command names

**Step 5 — Ask Claude:** *"What are the 5 most time-saving terminal techniques for someone using PowerShell in VS Code for [your work type]?"*

sections.title: Workshop B — Run a Real Project in the Terminal
sections.content:
Use the integrated terminal to run a complete project workflow from start to finish.

**Step 1 — Open your project** in VS Code.

**Step 2 — Run these project commands** from the integrated terminal (adapting to your project type):

For Python:
```powershell
python --version
python main.py
```

For Node.js:
```powershell
node --version
npm install
node index.js
```

For any project:
```powershell
git status
git log --oneline
```

**Step 3 — If you encounter an error**, paste it directly to Claude from the terminal. Ask: "I got this error while running [command] in VS Code's integrated terminal: [paste error]. What does it mean and how do I fix it?"

**Step 4 — Install a dependency** from the terminal (Python example):
```powershell
pip install requests
```

**Step 5 — Verify the dependency works** by writing a 3-line Python script that imports it.

sections.title: Workshop C — Terminal Profiles and Customisation
sections.content:
Set up your terminal to be faster and more informative.

**Step 1 — Check what shells are available:**
```powershell
# In PowerShell:
Get-Command -Name pwsh, bash, zsh 2>$null
```

**Step 2 — Install Windows Terminal** (if on Windows): it's a better terminal than the default cmd. Install from Microsoft Store.

**Step 3 — Configure VS Code terminal settings:**
Open Settings (Ctrl+,) → search "terminal" → configure:
- `terminal.integrated.fontSize`: set to a comfortable size
- `terminal.integrated.cursorBlinking`: enable
- `terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.windows`: set to PowerShell

**Step 4 — Install Oh My Posh** (optional but impactful): It adds a theme to your PowerShell prompt that shows git branch, Python environment, and other useful context. Ask Claude: "How do I install Oh My Posh for PowerShell to improve my terminal experience?"

**Step 5 — Test your improved terminal** by navigating into a git repository and noticing the branch name shown in your prompt.

sections.title: Workshop D — Terminal Automation Script
sections.content:
Automate your project startup with a script that runs from the VS Code terminal.

**Step 1 — Identify your project startup sequence** — the commands you run at the start of every work session: activating a virtual environment, starting a server, running initial checks.

**Step 2 — Ask Claude:** *"Create a PowerShell/bash script called `start.ps1` (or `start.sh`) that automates my project startup. The script should: [describe your startup sequence]. After each step, it should print a confirmation message so I know it succeeded."*

**Step 3 — Create and test the script** from the VS Code terminal.

**Step 4 — Add it to your VS Code Task:**
In .vscode/tasks.json, add a task that runs your startup script:
```json
{
    "label": "Start Project",
    "type": "shell",
    "command": ".\\start.ps1",
    "group": "build"
}
```

**Step 5 — Mandatory review:** Ask Claude: *"Review this startup script. What could cause it to fail on a different machine or after a system update? What should I add to make it more robust?"*

sections.question: You're running a Python server in VS Code's terminal and it's stuck — it won't accept new commands. How do you stop it?
options: Close VS Code and reopen it
Press Ctrl+C — this sends an interrupt signal to stop the running process
Close the terminal tab — this kills the process
sections.explanation: Ctrl+C sends an interrupt signal (SIGINT) to the running process, which is the standard way to stop servers, scripts, or any running terminal program gracefully. Most well-written programs handle this by cleaning up and shutting down. Ctrl+Z suspends the process (it continues running in the background). Closing the terminal tab (C) does also kill the process but is less clean.

sections.question: You have three terminals open in VS Code running different things: one running your server, one for git commands, and one for running tests. How do you switch between them?
options: You can only have one terminal open at a time
Click the terminal names in the terminal dropdown panel
sections.explanation: VS Code's integrated terminal panel shows multiple terminals as separate tabs or entries in a dropdown. Click the name/number of the terminal you want to switch to. You can also use the dropdown arrow next to the terminal panel header to see all active terminals. Keeping multiple terminals open (server, git, tests) is a standard professional workflow — you don't need to stop and restart between tasks.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 5-7.** The integrated terminal is now a core part of your workflow. You'll use it constantly throughout this course — it's how you run Git commands, install Node packages, launch Claude Code, and much more. Next: the VS Code Extensions Marketplace.

**Across industries:**

- Retail & Hospitality: A revenue analyst runs a nightly pricing script from the integrated terminal and pastes any error straight to AI without switching windows.
- Consulting & Professional Services: A consultant runs client data-cleaning scripts and git commands from one terminal pane during a live workshop.
- Healthcare: A health-informatics analyst runs de-identification scripts against patient extracts, keeping code and output side by side.
- Legal: A legal-ops analyst runs a document-batch-renaming script from the terminal while reviewing the affected files in the same window.
- Finance/Accounting: A financial analyst runs a reconciliation script and installs a missing package mid-task without ever leaving the editor.
